questions.title: T-shaped pendulum and damped oscillations
questions.summary: Masses on the cross-bar change the moment of inertia: T² = ax² + b. Add your own points to the printed graph, find a and b, test how they depend on M, plan how b depends on h and w, and analyse a velocity–time dataset of a damped oscillation.

xlsx.desc: The four printed points plus two sample readings. Fit T² against x².
A practice version of datasetQ1g: horizontal velocity every 0.02 s. Find a (gradient) and s (cumulative area), plot a against s, and find ω, the amplitude and the damping ratio.

questions.title: Friction on a strip leaning on a smooth board
questions.summary: A strip leans on a smooth vertical board at the angle where it just stops slipping. F = (M/2 + Sd/L)/((M + S) tan θ) is the friction coefficient; compare F with the mass low (A) and high (B) for two strips.

questions.title: Two wires in series via a sliding lead
questions.summary: Current flows along length x of wire F, through lead C, and along (L − x) of wire G. 1/I = Px + Q, and P/Q = (d_G²/d_F² − 1)/L lets you find the diameter ratio from the graph.

xlsx.desc: Seven (x, I) pairs. Plot 1/I against x, find P and Q, then d_G/d_F.

notes.text: Name the method AND the spreadsheet operation: gradient (central difference) for a; cumulative area (trapezium) for s.
For SHM a = −ω²x. Since s is measured from the release point, the graph of a against s has gradient −ω² but does not pass through the origin.
Use only the first few cycles for the fit: damping slowly shrinks the oscillation.

8.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="140.0" y="119.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Peak speeds in successive cycles are proportional to the amplitudes:</text><text x="140.0" y="131.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">v₁ = 0.1919, v₂ = 0.1803, v₃ = 0.1689, v₄ = 0.1590 m s⁻¹</text><text x="140.0" y="143.1" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">ratios: 0.940, 0.937, 0.941 → mean</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q1"><text x="364.9" y="240.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.939</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Constant ratio A(n+1)/A(n) means exponential damping. Use peak speeds (or peak displacements) of consecutive cycles.

9.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="365.2" y="158.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">50.0 cm</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="364.9" y="392.3" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">10.0 cm</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Strip lengths to 0.1 cm with a metre rule; d is measured to the centre of the slotted mass.

10.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="364.9" y="207.5" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">37°</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="140.0" y="259.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Repeated trials gave 36°, 38°, 37°: the "just stays" position is a judgement</text><text x="140.0" y="271.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Δθ ≈ 2°</text><text x="140.0" y="283.1" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">% uncertainty = 2/37 × 100%</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="364.9" y="359.2" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">5%</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="364.9" y="440.6" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">45.2 g</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="140.0" y="569.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">F_A = (0.0452/2 + 0.100 × 10.0/50.0) / ((0.0452 + 0.100) tan 37°)</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="364.9" y="702.9" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">0.39</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Measure θ at the bottom of the strip with a protractor on the bench, or measure height and base and use tan θ = height/base.
The limiting position varies between trials. Repeat it and use the spread for Δθ.
F is dimensionless (it is the coefficient of static friction between strip and bench). Use consistent mass units.

13.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 612.00 792.00" font-family="DejaVu Sans, Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif"><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="119.0" y="183.3" font-size="8.8" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">% difference in k = 13%. k depends on two angles each with ≈ 5% uncertainty, so k is</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="119.0" y="206.3" font-size="8.8" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">uncertain by roughly 2 × 5% = 11% (or more, since tan θ is involved). 13% is outside</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="119.0" y="229.8" font-size="8.8" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">this, so the results do not support F_A/F_B = k.</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="303.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">The friction varies along the bench and the "just stays" position is hard to</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="327.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">judge, so θ is hard to reproduce (the strip may stay at slightly different angles</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="351.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">in repeat trials).</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="438.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">Place the strip on a rough board of uniform surface fixed to the bench and</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="462.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">slowly tilt the board/strip; or measure the height of the top end and the</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="486.2" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">horizontal distance with a rule and use tan θ = height/distance, repeating 5</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="139.0" y="509.7" font-size="9.2" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">times and averaging.</text></g></svg>

notes.text: Use the % uncertainty you calculated in (a)(iii); compare it with the % difference in k.
Avoid "human error". Name the specific difficulty: judging the limiting position, or friction varying along the bench.

notes.text: Average several micrometer readings at different points and orientations; check the zero error first.
Open the switch between readings: the wire heats up and its resistance changes.
Seven values over the whole wire (10–90 cm). Record I to the ammeter's precision, and 1/I to 3 s.f.
Units: P in A⁻¹ m⁻¹ if x is in metres (A⁻¹ cm⁻¹ if in cm). Be consistent with L = 1.000 m in (d).
